Where it began

Malcolm Marshall was born in Bridgetown, Barbados, on 18 April 1958, and was raised in Saint Michael parish. His grandfather helped to bring him up and gave him some of his early cricket lessons. His boyhood hero was Garfield Sobers.

He was playing for the Banks Brewery team when his break arrived. His first-class debut, for Barbados against Jamaica in February 1978, brought him 6 for 77, and on the strength of that one game he was chosen to tour India. He heard the news on the radio at work, and later owned up to having no real idea where India was.

The player

His first Test came at Bangalore in December 1978. After 1980/81 he went two years without a Test. Hampshire, his county since 1979, got the benefit: in 1982 he took 134 first-class wickets for them, and by 2026 nobody had taken more in an English season since the county programme was trimmed in 1969. West Indies recalled him for good.

From 1982/83 to 1985/86 he took at least 21 wickets in seven Test series in a row. In India in 1983/84 he claimed 33 and made his best Test score, 92 at Kanpur. His finest figures, 7 for 22, came at Old Trafford in 1988, in a summer that brought him 35 wickets at 12.65. In 81 Tests he took 376 wickets at 20.95, with 22 five-wicket innings and four ten-wicket matches.

What made him special

He was shorter than most of the fast men of his day, yet his action gave him real pace and his bouncer kept batsmen honest. As the years went on he added swing in both directions, a leg-cutter and an in-swinging yorker. He rose to the top of the ICC Test bowling rankings in 1989 and held that place through 1990.

He could bat, too, with ten Test fifties. A Test hundred never quite arrived, though seven first-class centuries suggest he always had one in him.

Away from the middle

He stayed with Hampshire until 1993, took 1,065 wickets for them and was part of the side that won the Benson and Hedges Cup in 1992. Later, at Natal, his experience helped shape the young Shaun Pollock. In 1996 he took charge of coaching Hampshire and the West Indies at the same time.

Wisden made him a Cricketer of the Year and when the Almanack turned 150 it named him in its all-time World Test team. He joined the ICC Cricket Hall of Fame in 2009. He died in 1999, aged 41. The leading wicket-taker in each Test series between England and West Indies receives a trophy in his name, and the approach road at Hampshire's Rose Bowl is Marshall Drive, named for him and for Roy Marshall.

And finally

He was in the West Indies squad that won the 1979 World Cup without playing a match in it, surely the most restful way to become a world champion. And in a benefit game at Southampton in 1993 the fast bowler took the wicket of David Gower with off-spin.
